title: Revenue
description: Class 11 Economics: total revenue, average revenue and marginal revenue, the relationship between TR, AR and MR, and the revenue curves under perfect and imperfect competition.

topics.title: Total, Average and Marginal Revenue
topics.concept:
Just as a firm has costs of production, it also earns revenue from selling its output. Revenue is the money a firm receives from selling its goods. There are three measures, parallel to the cost measures:

  • Total Revenue (TR) — the total money received from selling a given quantity of output: TR = Price × Quantity (P × Q).
  • Average Revenue (AR) — revenue per unit sold: AR = TR ÷ Q. Since TR = P × Q, dividing by Q gives AR = P. So average revenue is the same as the price of the good. This is why the AR curve is also the firm's demand curve.
  • Marginal Revenue (MR) — the addition to total revenue from selling one more unit: MR = change in TR (TRₙ − TRₙ₋₁).

For example, if a firm sells 10 units at ₹5 each, its TR = 5 × 10 = ₹50, and its AR = 50 ÷ 10 = ₹5 (= the price). If selling the 11th unit raises TR from ₹50 to ₹54, the MR of that unit = 54 − 50 = ₹4. These three revenue concepts, together with the cost concepts, are what a producer compares to decide how much to produce.

examples.problem: Example 1: Write the formulas for total, average and marginal revenue.
examples.solution:
One total, one per-unit, one extra.

  • TR = Price × Quantity.
  • AR = TR ÷ Q (= price); MR = change in TR.
examples.answer: TR = P × Q; AR = TR ÷ Q (= price); MR = change in TR (TRₙ − TRₙ₋₁).

examples.problem: Example 2: A firm sells 8 units at ₹12 each. Find TR and AR.
Example 3: Why is average revenue equal to the price of the good?
examples.solution:
Start from TR = P × Q.

  • AR = TR ÷ Q = (P × Q) ÷ Q = P.
examples.answer: Because AR = TR ÷ Q = (P × Q) ÷ Q = P, so average revenue always equals the price.

recap:
• TR = P × Q; AR = TR ÷ Q = Price (so the AR curve is the demand curve); MR = change in TR.
  • A firm compares revenue with cost to decide its output.

quiz.q: Average revenue is always equal to the:
quiz.explanation: AR = TR ÷ Q = P, so AR equals the price.

topics.title: Relationship between TR, AR and MR
topics.concept:
The three revenue measures are linked, and their relationship depends on whether the price stays the same as more is sold.

When price is constant (the firm can sell any quantity at the same price — as under perfect competition):

  • AR = MR = Price (all equal and constant).
  • TR rises in a straight line as output rises.

When price falls as more is sold (the firm must lower price to sell more — as under monopoly/imperfect competition):

  • AR falls as output rises (the AR/demand curve slopes downward).
  • MR falls faster and lies below AR.
  • TR rises, reaches a maximum (where MR = 0), and then falls.

The general links: TR = AR × Q; AR = TR ÷ Q; and MR is the change in TR. A useful rule connects MR to TR: when MR is positive, TR is rising; when MR = 0, TR is maximum; when MR is negative, TR is falling. This relationship (especially MR = 0 at maximum TR) is important later when we find the producer's profit-maximising output, where the firm balances marginal revenue against marginal cost.

examples.problem: Example 1: When the price is constant, what is the relationship between AR and MR?
examples.solution:
They are equal and constant.

  • AR = MR = Price.
examples.answer: When price is constant, AR = MR = price (both equal and constant).

examples.problem: Example 2: When a firm must lower price to sell more, how do AR and MR behave?
examples.solution:
Both fall, MR faster.

  • AR (the demand curve) slopes downward.
  • MR falls faster and lies below AR.
examples.answer: Both fall as output rises; AR slopes downward and MR falls faster, lying below AR.

examples.problem: Example 3: Total revenue is maximum when marginal revenue is:
examples.solution:
Recall the TR–MR link.

  • TR is maximum when MR = 0.
  • Beyond that, MR is negative and TR falls.
examples.answer: When MR = 0 (TR is maximum at that point).

recap:
• Constant price (perfect competition): AR = MR = Price; TR a straight rising line.
  • Falling price (imperfect competition): AR falls (downward curve), MR below AR and falls faster.
  • TR & MR link: MR > 0 → TR rising; MR = 0 → TR maximum; MR < 0 → TR falling.

quiz.q: When price is constant, AR and MR are:
options: Equal to each other and to price
quiz.explanation: With constant price, AR = MR = price.

quiz.q: Total revenue is maximum when marginal revenue is:
quiz.explanation: TR is maximum at the output where MR = 0.

topics.title: Revenue Curves: Perfect vs Imperfect Competition
topics.concept:
The shape of a firm's revenue curves depends on the market in which it sells.

Under perfect competition, a single firm is so small that it cannot influence the market price — it is a price taker and can sell any quantity at the ruling price. So its price is constant, which means AR = MR = Price, and the AR (and MR) curve is a horizontal straight line parallel to the X-axis at the level of the price.

Under imperfect competition (monopoly, monopolistic competition), a firm has some control over price and must lower its price to sell more. So its AR (demand) curve slopes downward, and its MR curve also slopes downward but lies below the AR curve. The diagrams below show the contrast:

examples.problem: Example 1: Why are AR and MR equal and horizontal under perfect competition?
examples.solution:
The firm is a price taker.

  • It can sell any quantity at the same ruling price.
  • So price is constant, AR = MR = price, and the curve is horizontal.
examples.answer: Because the firm is a price taker selling at a constant price, so AR = MR = price, giving a horizontal line.

examples.problem: Example 2: Under imperfect competition, how do the AR and MR curves look?
examples.solution:
The firm lowers price to sell more.

  • AR (demand) slopes downward.
  • MR also slopes downward but lies below AR.
examples.answer: Both slope downward; the MR curve lies below the downward-sloping AR (demand) curve.

examples.solution:
The firm accepts the market price.

  • A firm too small to affect the market price; it sells at the price set by the market.
examples.answer: A firm that cannot influence the market price and must accept (take) the price set by the market.

recap:
• Perfect competition: firm is a price taker; AR = MR = Price; revenue curve is a horizontal line.
  • Imperfect competition: firm lowers price to sell more; AR slopes downward and MR lies below AR.

quiz.q: Under perfect competition, a firm's AR curve is:
quiz.explanation: A price-taking firm has a horizontal AR = MR = price line.

quiz.q: Under imperfect competition, the MR curve lies:
quiz.explanation: When price must fall to sell more, MR lies below the downward AR curve.

questions.q: Average revenue is:
questions.explanation: AR = TR ÷ Q.

questions.q: Average revenue is always equal to the:
questions.explanation: AR = TR ÷ Q = P, so AR equals the price.

questions.q: The AR curve of a firm is the same as its:
questions.explanation: Since AR = price, the AR curve is the demand curve.

questions.q: Marginal revenue is the:
options: Change in TR from one more unit
questions.explanation: MR = change in total revenue from selling one more unit.

When price is constant, AR and MR are:
questions.explanation: With constant price, AR = MR = price.

questions.q: When a firm must lower its price to sell more, the AR curve:
questions.explanation: Lowering price to sell more gives a downward-sloping AR curve.

questions.q: When price falls to sell more, the MR curve lies:
questions.explanation: MR lies below the downward AR curve under imperfect competition.

questions.q: Total revenue is maximum when marginal revenue is:
questions.explanation: TR is maximum at the output where MR = 0.

questions.q: When MR is positive, total revenue is:
questions.explanation: Positive MR means TR is still rising.

questions.q: A firm that cannot influence the market price is a:
questions.explanation: Under perfect competition the firm is a price taker.

questions.q: Under perfect competition, the AR = MR curve is:
questions.explanation: Constant price gives a horizontal AR = MR line.

questions.q: If TR rises from ₹96 to ₹105 when one more unit is sold, MR is:
A wheat farmer in a perfectly competitive market can sell any amount at the going price of ₹20/kg. For him, AR and MR are:
questions.explanation: As a price taker, his AR = MR = price = ₹20, constant at every quantity.

questions.q: TR values for 1, 2, 3 units are ₹10, ₹18, ₹24. The MR of the 3rd unit is:
questions.explanation: MR₃ = TR₃ − TR₂ = 24 − 18 = ₹6.

questions.q: Because AR equals price, the firm's AR curve is identical to its:
questions.explanation: AR = price at each quantity, which is exactly what the demand curve shows.

questions.q: A monopolist's MR is below its AR because, to sell an extra unit, it must:
options: Lower the price on all units sold
questions.explanation: Cutting the price to sell one more unit reduces revenue on the earlier units too, so MR falls below AR.

questions.q: As a firm with a downward demand curve keeps increasing sales, TR will eventually:
options: Reach a maximum (where MR = 0) and then fall
questions.explanation: TR peaks where MR = 0; beyond that MR is negative and TR declines.

questions.q: If selling more units leaves total revenue unchanged, the marginal revenue of those units is:
questions.explanation: No change in TR means each extra unit adds nothing — MR = 0.

questions.q: The horizontal AR = MR line of a competitive firm reflects that the firm is:
options: Too small to affect the market price
questions.explanation: Being a tiny price taker, it sells all it wants at the fixed market price.

questions.q: For a firm under imperfect competition, which is true?
options: MR < AR at every positive output
questions.explanation: With a downward demand curve, marginal revenue always lies below average revenue.

questions.q: A shop earns ₹500 selling 50 pens. Its average revenue (price) per pen is:
questions.explanation: AR = TR ÷ Q = 500 ÷ 50 = ₹10, which is the price.

questions.q: The link MR = 0 at maximum TR becomes important in the next chapter because producers maximise profit by comparing MR with:
questions.explanation: Profit is maximised where MR = MC, so the revenue side (MR) is matched against the cost side (MC).
